title: Woody 'Blankets' Tested on Arctic Permafrost to Cut Emissions
title_zh: 用木质“毯子”盖住北极冻土，能减少碳排放吗？

image.credit: U.S. Department of Energy · cc0 1.0 · via rawpixel

lead: A Canadian start-up is testing whether insulating blankets made from woody materials can stop rapidly eroding permafrost from releasing greenhouse gases. Early results look promising, but scientists say more testing is needed.

paragraphs: A Canadian start-up called PermaC is developing a way to prevent greenhouse-gas emissions from permafrost by covering the soil with an insulating 'blanket' made of woody materials. If the method works, it could be the first tool to directly stop emissions that escape from permafrost as the Arctic heats up. 'Our goal is to make sure the carbon in the soil remains buried,' says Cansu Culha, co-founder of PermaC and a researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada.

Earth's frozen environments are thawing as temperatures rise because of human emissions. The only reliable way to slow this melting on a global scale is to cut emissions from burning fossil fuels. However, some researchers are exploring methods to prevent the thaw directly, such as placing reflective mats on glaciers or pumping water onto sea ice to thicken it. Researchers say PermaC's approach is the first they know of to focus on preventing permafrost thaw and its associated emissions, which are estimated to be equivalent to those of Japan.

The company has just completed the first test of its insulating blankets in Canada's Northwest Territories, at an area of rapidly eroding permafrost known as a retrogressive thaw slump. These slumps occur when a hill of permafrost thaws and collapses, allowing erosion to take big bites out of the landscape. This exposes deeper layers of soil to warming, forming hotspots of CO2 and methane emissions. One estimate suggests that these areas of rapid erosion could amplify permafrost emissions by as much as 40% compared to models that only account for gradual thaw.

The company's approach is to stabilize the edge of the slumps with a layer of wood shavings, soil and native seeds, and a burlap-like mat of coconut husks. Culha says she got the idea after hearing about Indigenous communities in Alaska that prevent permafrost degradation by planting trees along the edges of slumps. Similar erosion-control blankets are used in temperate areas, but they haven't been used to insulate or stabilize permafrost until now, she says. PermaC has not yet released results from this year's test, but the blanket seems to have halted erosion: over the Arctic summer, the edge of the slump without the blanket retreated by 5 metres, whereas the blanketed area saw no measurable retreat, Culha says.

'That's very promising,' says Christina Schaedel, a permafrost scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Falmouth, Massachusetts, who has been advising the company. However, she adds that the result is from only one slump over one summer. One challenge is calculating how much CO2 the blankets prevent from being emitted. Measuring the CO2 emissions from slumps is not straightforward and remains an active research question, says Mark Lara, a biologist at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. 'There definitely are slumps that are spewing out carbon,' he says, but there are 'lots of minutiae that could dramatically impact the results', he adds.

So far, Culha has only rough estimates for the emissions that the blankets might prevent. Extrapolating from research on erosion rates and soil carbon in the Arctic, she thinks that about 2,200 tonnes of CO2 a year might be prevented from being emitted at the average carbon-rich slump. If those calculations are accurate and the blankets can be installed at 20,000 slumps across Canada and Alaska — the company's ambitious goal over the next decade — she estimates that they might prevent about 40 million tonnes of CO2 emissions a year, roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of Hungary. Culha says the company is developing a detailed methodology that a third party could use to verify prevented emissions, which would be necessary for the company to sell carbon credits. The firm aims to issue credits as soon as next year, and has so far raised Can$1.4 million (US$1 million) from investors.
paragraphs_zh: 一家名为PermaC的加拿大初创公司正在开发一种方法，通过用木质材料制成的保温“毯子”覆盖土壤，来防止永久冻土释放温室气体。如果这种方法有效，它可能是第一个直接阻止随着北极变暖而从永久冻土中逸出的排放的工具。PermaC联合创始人、加拿大温哥华不列颠哥伦比亚大学的研究员坎苏·库尔哈说：“我们的目标是确保土壤中的碳继续埋在地下。”
随着人类排放导致气温上升，地球的冰冻环境正在融化。在全球范围内减缓这种融化的唯一可靠方法是减少燃烧化石燃料产生的排放。然而，一些研究人员正在探索直接防止融化的方法，例如在冰川上放置反射垫，或将水抽到海冰上使其变厚。研究人员表示，据他们所知，PermaC的方法是第一个专注于防止永久冻土融化及其相关排放的方法，这些排放估计相当于日本的排放量。
该公司刚刚在加拿大西北地区完成了其保温毯的首次测试，测试地点是一片快速侵蚀的永久冻土区域，被称为后退式热融滑塌。当永久冻土的山丘融化并坍塌时，就会发生这种滑塌，使侵蚀对景观造成大面积破坏。这使更深层的土壤暴露在变暖中，形成二氧化碳和甲烷排放的热点。一项估计表明，与仅考虑逐渐融化的模型相比，这些快速侵蚀区域可能会使永久冻土排放量增加多达40%。

该公司的做法是用一层木屑、土壤和本地种子，以及类似粗麻布的椰子壳垫子来稳定滑塌的边缘。库尔哈说，她是在听说阿拉斯加的土著社区通过在滑塌边缘种树来防止永久冻土退化后产生了这个想法。她说，类似的侵蚀控制毯在温带地区也有使用，但直到现在才被用于隔离或稳定永久冻土。PermaC尚未公布今年测试的结果，但毯子似乎已经阻止了侵蚀：库尔哈说，在北极夏季，没有毯子的滑塌边缘后退了5米，而有毯子的区域没有测量到后退。

“这非常有希望，”马萨诸塞州法尔茅斯伍德韦尔气候研究中心的永久冻土科学家克里斯蒂娜·谢德尔说，她一直在为该公司提供建议。然而，她补充说，这一结果仅来自一个滑塌和一个夏季。一个挑战是计算毯子防止了多少二氧化碳排放。伊利诺伊大学厄巴纳-香槟分校研究永久冻土景观的生物学家马克·拉拉说，测量滑塌的二氧化碳排放并不简单，仍然是一个活跃的研究问题。“确实有滑塌在排放碳，”他说，但“有很多细节可能会极大地影响结果”，他补充道。

到目前为止，库尔哈对毯子可能防止的排放只有粗略的估计。根据对北极侵蚀率和土壤碳的研究进行推断，她认为在平均富含碳的滑塌中，每年可能防止约2200吨二氧化碳的排放。如果这些计算准确，并且毯子可以安装在加拿大和阿拉斯加的20000个滑塌中——该公司未来十年的雄心勃勃的目标——她估计它们每年可能防止约4000万吨二氧化碳排放，大致相当于匈牙利的年排放量。库尔哈说，该公司正在制定一种详细的方法，第三方可以用它来验证防止的排放，这对于公司出售碳信用额是必要的。该公司计划最早在明年发行信用额，并且迄今为止已从投资者那里筹集了140万加元（100万美元）。
